detail.organize: Use the organizer when the document itself is fine and only the sequence is wrong: a scan stitched from two passes, a contract whose signature page ended up at the back, a proposal with the appendix in the middle. Unlike merging, nothing is combined here, so the page count only changes when you add blank pages or pull pages in from another file. Organizing is about sequence, not content, so it is the wrong tool when pages have to come from several documents at once — that is merge's job. What it does offer is mixing: pages from a second file can be pulled into the new order, and blank pages inserted to separate sections. The page count changes only when you add or remove a page, never when you reorder.
detail.merge: Merging fits when the information already lives in separate files and belongs in one: a folder of supplier invoices, chapters exported one by one, a contract plus its annex. Every page keeps its original size, so mixing A4 and Letter is allowed but looks uneven once printed. Two things surprise people the first time. Page sizes are not normalised, so an A4 contract merged with a Letter annex prints at two different widths — resize one side first if the result goes to a printer. And document-level bookmarks are not carried over: the pages survive intact, but the navigation outline has to be rebuilt. If you only need pages from a single file in a different order, the page editor is the lighter choice than merging a file with itself.
detail.split: Split is for handing over part of a document without exposing the rest: one chapter to a reviewer, a single invoice to accounting, the signed pages to a counterparty. Break points sit between pages, so if a section starts in the middle of a page, crop it first and split the result. Splitting does not renumber anything: pages keep their original labels, so a chapter cut from pages 40-58 still reads 40-58 in its footer, and renumbering is a separate step. Break points are inserted between pages, which means a section that begins mid-page cannot be separated cleanly — crop that page first, then split the cropped file. A file that still carries an open password has to be unlocked before any page can be read.
detail.rotate: Rotate is a repair tool: it changes orientation and nothing else. A sheet fed upside down, a photo of a form saved sideways, a landscape table inside a portrait report. Only a rotation flag is written, so the text stays selectable and the file size does not change. Only the orientation flag is rewritten, which is why this is safe on a file you will keep working with: text stays selectable, images keep their resolution and the file size does not move. It is not a fix for a scan that was fed slightly crooked — a small tilt needs deskewing, which rotation in 90-degree steps cannot do. When only a few pages are wrong, select them instead of rotating the document. Landscape pages inside a portrait document are the common case: select those pages rather than rotating everything, or the pages that were already correct will come out sideways.
detail.reorderPages: The page editor is for re-sequencing a document you already have: every page appears as a thumbnail, which makes a missing or duplicated scan easy to spot. It works on one file at a time; when the pages come from several documents, use organize or merge instead. Every page is drawn as a thumbnail, which makes this the quickest way to spot a duplicate or a missing scan before a document goes out. It works on one file at a time, so when the pages live in several documents, organize or merge is the right tool. Thumbnails are rendered on the fly, so a file with a few hundred pages takes a moment to fill in. A quick way to verify the order before exporting is to compare the last page of one section against the first page of the next; the thumbnail grid turns that check into a glance rather than a scroll.
detail.deletePages: Reach for delete when a document is mostly right but carries pages that should not travel with it: a blank reverse side, a superseded quote, an internal cover sheet. Nothing is written until you export, so an accidental removal costs nothing more than reloading the file. Deleting is safe to experiment with because nothing is written until you export: deselect the page, or reload the file, and it comes back. The range field and the odd/even shortcut exist for two-sided scans, where every blank reverse has to go and clicking a hundred times is not an option. A document where only a handful of pages should survive is usually faster to handle with extract than with delete. On a long document, check the range field against the thumbnail row before exporting: a mistyped range such as 4-12 instead of 4-21 removes more pages than intended, and the export is where that becomes visible.
detail.extractPages: Extract is the inverse of delete: instead of removing pages you keep only the ones you name. Pull an invoice out of a statement, an annex out of a contract, a chapter out of a manual — as one new PDF or as a ZIP with one file per page. Extract is the mirror of delete: you name what stays instead of what goes. That makes it the better choice for a 300-page statement where one invoice matters, or a manual where one chapter does. The output is either a single PDF holding the selected pages in their original order, or a ZIP with one file per page — the second is what you want when each page has to be sent somewhere different. Watch the page count when the selection is large: a ZIP of three hundred single-page files takes longer to unpack than one PDF holding the same pages, and most recipients would rather receive the single file.
detail.crop: Cropping narrows the visible area without rewriting the page, so text inside the frame stays selectable. It is the honest fix for a scanner border, an over-wide slide export or a browser header baked in by print-to-PDF; whatever sits outside the frame is hidden rather than deleted, which is why the file size barely moves. The frame narrows the visible page; whatever falls outside is hidden rather than deleted, which is why the file size barely moves and why a crop can be widened again later. It is the right fix for a scanner border or a browser header baked in by print-to-PDF. It is the wrong fix for removing something nobody should read — that needs redaction, because the characters are still in the file. If the document will be signed or printed, keep the page number and any signature block inside the frame; clipping either is far easier to catch in the preview than after the file has been sent.
detail.edit: The editor covers small additions to a finished PDF: filling a field on a non-interactive form, signing without a printer, covering an old address before a document is forwarded. It does not reflow text — additions sit on top of the page, so a long replacement sentence may not fit the space the original occupied. Additions are drawn on top of the page rather than woven into its text layer, which has two consequences worth knowing before you start. A replacement sentence longer than the space it covers will overlap whatever sits beside it, so keep edits short or place them in a margin. And a white-out block hides text visually while leaving the original characters in the file — if the document must not contain the old value at all, it has to be redacted rather than covered.
detail.pdfToImage: Convert to an image when the destination cannot display a PDF: a chat app, a slide deck, a CMS upload field. Rendering happens at the resolution you choose, so 150 DPI suits screens and chat, 300 DPI is what print and OCR want, and higher settings only inflate the file. Pick the resolution by where the image is going, not by the biggest number on offer: 150 DPI is sharp on a screen at normal zoom, 300 DPI is what print and OCR expect, and anything above that mostly adds megabytes. A page rendered at 300 DPI carries roughly four times the pixels of the same page at 150, so a long document becomes a large download quickly. If the images will be placed back into a printed document, keep the resolution and the physical page size in mind together: a page rendered at 300 DPI only prints at A4 when it is placed at A4 dimensions.
detail.imageToPdf: Image-to-PDF is the return trip: photos of receipts, exported design frames, screenshots of a conversation. Because each page is built from an image, the exported file has no searchable text — run OCR on the result if the document has to be indexed or quoted. Every page of the result is a picture, so the PDF carries no text layer: it looks right and prints right, but it cannot be searched or quoted from. If the document has to be indexed, run OCR on the finished file. Setting a page size and margin matters more than it looks — photos of receipts dropped in at native size produce a document far bigger than A4 and awkward to print. A photographed contract stays unsearchable whatever page size you pick — OCR is the only way to add a text layer once a picture becomes a PDF.
detail.compress: Use this when a PDF is too heavy to send or store and you can accept a trade-off. Lossless rewriting only repacks the file structure: text stays selectable and nothing visible changes, but a document exported by recent software has little redundancy left, so a few percent is a normal outcome. The image levels re-render every page as a JPEG, which is what actually shrinks a scan and also what turns its text into a picture. Compress the copy you are about to print or attach and keep the original for anything you may still need to search or edit. The honest expectation matters more here than anywhere else. A file exported by Word or a modern scanner is already compressed internally, so the lossless level typically returns single-digit percentages; a file assembled from uncompressed scans can drop by half. The image levels are the ones that visibly shrink a page, and they do it by replacing the page with a picture — fine for a print copy, wrong for an archive you still need to search, quote or copy text out of.

organize.q: Does reorganizing reduce the file quality?
organize.a: No. Pages are copied as they are, so text, images and resolution stay identical; only the order and any inserted blank pages differ.

organize.q: Can I organize a password-protected PDF?
organize.a: You have to unlock it first. Showing a preview means reading every page, and an encrypted document cannot be read without its password.

merge.q: Are page sizes normalised when files are merged?
merge.a: No. Each page keeps its own dimensions, so A4 and Letter can sit in the same document and still print at their original sizes.

merge.q: What happens to bookmarks after merging?
merge.a: Page content is preserved in full, but document-level bookmarks are not carried into the new file; they have to be added again.

split.q: How are the split files named?
split.a: The original file name plus a part number, packaged in one ZIP so a single download delivers every part.

split.q: What happens to pages no break point covers?
split.a: They stay in their own part and are never dropped; only the boundaries you place between pages cut the document.

rotate.q: Can I rotate only one page of many?
rotate.a: Yes. Rotation is stored per page, so you can straighten a single sideways sheet and leave the rest untouched.
No. The page content is not re-rendered, so resolution, fonts and images are identical before and after.

reorderPages.q: Does it work on very long documents?
reorderPages.a: Thumbnails are rendered in the browser, so a file with several hundred pages takes a moment to fill in — most noticeably on a phone.

reorderPages.q: Can I rotate a page while reordering?
reorderPages.a: Yes. Rotation is stored per page, so one crooked scan can be corrected without affecting the others.

deletePages.q: Can I delete a whole range at once?
deletePages.a: Use the range field for a block such as 4-12, or the odd/even shortcut to strip every other page from a two-sided scan.

deletePages.q: Does deleting pages make the file smaller?
deletePages.a: Yes. Removed pages are not written to the export at all, so cutting a 200-page file down to 20 pages shrinks it considerably.

extractPages.q: Can the extracted pages be reordered?
extractPages.a: They keep their original order. If you need a different sequence, run the result through the page editor afterwards.

extractPages.q: Is text still selectable in the extracted pages?
extractPages.a: Yes. Pages are copied rather than re-rendered, so text, fonts and annotations survive intact.

crop.q: Is the cropped area really gone?
crop.a: It no longer prints and no longer shows, because the visible page box is narrowed. The underlying content is not rewritten, which is why the file size hardly changes.

crop.q: Can different pages be cropped differently?
crop.a: Yes. Apply one frame to the whole document, or switch to the selected pages so each keeps its own crop.

edit.a: Yes. Draw or type a signature once, then place it on as many pages as the document needs.
No. Additions are layered over the page, so original text cannot be selected or rewritten — cover it with a white-out block if it has to disappear.

pdfToImage.a: 150 for screens and chat, 200 for slides, 300 for print or OCR. Higher values look sharper and make the files much larger.

pdfToImage.q: Can I convert only some pages?
pdfToImage.a: Yes. Export every page or only the ones you select, either as single downloads or as one ZIP.

imageToPdf.a: They are embedded without a second round of compression, so sharp photos stay sharp and the PDF grows with them — that is expected.

imageToPdf.q: Can one PDF mix page sizes?
imageToPdf.a: The size you pick applies to the whole batch. For mixed formats, build two PDFs and merge them so each page keeps its own size.

compress.q: Why did my file shrink so little?
compress.a: Lossless compression can only remove redundancy in how the file is stored. A modern tool has little left to remove, so a few percent is a normal result, not a failure.

compress.q: Does compressing remove metadata or permissions?
compress.a: The lossless level leaves both as they are. The image levels rebuild the document from rendered pages, so old metadata and permission flags do not carry over — handy for a scan that still names whoever scanned it.
